Series::angle¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::angle() const

What It Does¶

Returns the phase of each element, in radians, in the range (-pi, pi].

For a complex input it is atan2(imag, real) — the angle the number makes with the positive real axis. For a real input it follows the same atan2(0, x) convention: 0 for a positive value, pi for a negative value, and 0 at zero.

Together with abs(), angle() gives the polar form of a complex series, and pluss::series::polar rebuilds a complex series from magnitude and angle.

From Coordinates To Direction¶

A complex value x + yi contains two independent kinds of information: abs() measures how far it is from the origin, while angle() measures its direction. Scaling by a positive real number changes the magnitude but leaves the angle unchanged. Multiplying by a unit complex value rotates the angle.

The result is expressed in radians. The branch cut lies on the negative real axis: directions just above it approach +pi, while directions just below it approach -pi. Those directions are geometrically close even though their numeric angles differ by nearly 2*pi; use a phase-unwrapping operation before taking differences across that cut.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

Series The phase in radians. Shape is preserved; the dtype is float32 for a Complex64 / real float32 input and float64 for a Complex128 / real float64 input.

Gradient¶

angle() is differentiable.

  • On a complex input the backward follows the standard rule d(angle)/dz = i * conj(z) / |z|^2 (Wirtinger form), so a reverse pass produces a non-zero complex sensitivity.

  • On a real input the phase is piecewise constant (0 or pi), so its local slope is 0 everywhere it is defined. A reverse pass therefore returns a zero sensitivity rather than raising — the real and complex paths agree.

At the origin the phase is defined as 0 and the gradient is not mathematically meaningful; the backward returns 0 there too.

Examples¶

Example 1. The phase of a complex series.

auto z = pluss::make_series(
    {std::complex<float>{3, 4}, {-1, 0}, {0, 2}, {0, 0}});

pluss::series::print(std::cout, z.angle()) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float32, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[0.9273, 3.1416, 1.5708, 0.0000]

atan2(4, 3) = 0.9273, atan2(0, -1) = pi, atan2(2, 0) = pi/2, atan2(0, 0) = 0.

Example 2. On a real input, angle() is 0 for positive values and pi for negative ones.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({2.0, -3.0, 0.0}).angle()
) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 3.1416, 0.0000]

Example 3. The gradient on a real leaf is zero — the reverse pass succeeds and fills the sensitivity with 0.

auto a = pluss::make_series({2.0, -1.0});
a.tracks_slope_(true);
a.angle().sum().reverse();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, a.sensitivity()) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.0000, -0.0000]

Example 4. Axis-aligned values make the quadrants explicit. The fifth value, 3 + 4j, lies in the first quadrant; the origin is assigned phase zero.

auto z = pluss::series::complex(
    pluss::make_series({1.0f, 0.0f, -1.0f, 0.0f, 3.0f, 0.0f}),
    pluss::make_series({0.0f, 1.0f,  0.0f, -1.0f, 4.0f, 0.0f}));
pluss::series::print(std::cout, z.angle()) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[6], strides=[1], dtype=float32, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 1.5708, 3.1416, -1.5708, 0.9273, 0.0000]

Example 5. The complex sensitivity is easiest to understand in Cartesian coordinates. For z = x + yi,

d angle / dx = -y / (x^2 + y^2)
d angle / dy =  x / (x^2 + y^2)

At 3 + 4j, these are -4/25 and 3/25, represented together as -0.16 + 0.12j. The origin receives zero because no direction is defined there.

auto z = pluss::series::complex(
    pluss::make_series({3.0f, 0.0f}),
    pluss::make_series({4.0f, 0.0f}));
z.tracks_slope_(true);
z.angle().sum().reverse();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, z.sensitivity()) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=complex64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[(-0.1600+0.1200j), (0.0000+0.0000j)]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • The range is (-pi, pi]. angle() of a negative real is pi, not -pi.

  • A raw subtraction of wrapped phases is unsafe across the negative-real branch cut; values near +pi and -pi can represent nearby directions.

  • Result dtype tracks the input precision (Complex64 -> float32).

  • Integral and low-precision real inputs produce float32 radians; float64 and Complex128 produce float64.

  • On a real input the gradient is 0, not an error — do not treat a zero sensitivity here as a broken graph.

  • For the polar decomposition pair with abs() for the magnitude; rebuild with pluss::series::polar.

Summary¶

angle() is the phase of each element in radians:

  • atan2(imag, real) for complex, atan2(0, x) for real; range (-pi, pi]

  • differentiable: non-zero complex sensitivity on the complex path, exact zero on the real path (no raise)

  • pairs with abs() for polar form

  • preserves shape and returns radians, with a branch cut on the negative real axis

See Also¶

  • Series::abs: the magnitude — the other half of polar form.

  • Series::real / Series::imag: the Cartesian components angle() is built from.

  • pluss::series::polar / pluss::series::complex: build a complex series from magnitude/angle or real/imaginary parts.
